entities.summary:
Floris of Montmorency, Baron of Montigny (c. 1540 – October 24, 1570), was a prominent noble and diplomat from the Spanish Netherlands whose tragic fate ignited further resistance against Spanish rule during the tumultuous early years of the Dutch Revolt. As the younger brother of Philip de Montmorency, Count of Horn, Floris belonged to one of the most powerful and ancient aristocratic families in the Low Countries. His diplomatic mission to Spain, intended to bridge the chasm between the Dutch nobility and King Philip II, instead led to his prolonged imprisonment and eventual execution, transforming him into a martyr for the burgeoning Calvinist and nationalistic causes.

Montigny's pivotal role began in 1566 when, amidst growing unrest and the Iconoclastic Fury, he was dispatched to Madrid alongside John of Montmorency to present the grievances of the Dutch nobility directly to Philip II. Their mandate was to plead for the withdrawal of Spanish troops, an end to the harsh enforcement of the Inquisition, and a more lenient approach to religious policy. Initially, Philip II received Floris with apparent cordiality, but as news of further disturbances in the Netherlands reached Spain, the king's attitude hardened. Montigny found himself under increasing surveillance, effectively detained under house arrest, and later imprisoned in the castle of Segovia without formal trial.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Floris of Montmorency's diplomatic mission and subsequent execution served as a critical turning point, solidifying noble opposition and intensifying the Eighty Years' War. His fate, alongside his brother's, galvanized anti-Spanish sentiment and contributed to the eventual independence of the Dutch Republic.
